Engineering reference material:

# Study guide

Read [architecture](architecture.md), then trace `routes.py` -> `app/service.py` ->
`inference/scheduler/scheduler.py` -> `executor.py` -> `lfm3/model.py`, where
short-convolution and attention blocks alternate.

## Token budgets and fairness

Decode generates one token per selected request. Prefill processes a chunk and
usually offers larger matrix operations. A token budget bounds scheduled work,
not GPU elapsed time: token cost still depends on context and model dimensions.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Scheduler
    participant W as Model worker
    Note over S,W: Illustrative ordering, not measured timing
    S->>W: Prefill A, final chunk
    W-->>S: First token A
    S->>W: Decode A, budget minus 1
    W-->>S: Next token A
    S->>W: Prefill B, bounded chunk
    W-->>S: B still prefilling
    S->>W: Decode A
    W-->>S: Next token A
    S->>W: Prefill B, final chunk
    W-->>S: First token B
    S->>W: Ragged decode A + B
    W-->>S: One token per request
```

Explain why unconditional prefill priority starves decode, and why unconditional
decode priority can starve prefill. Locate both fairness tests. Explain why this
implementation uses separate forwards rather than a fused mixed batch.

## Page sharing and memory

![Illustrative page sharing and analytical capacity](figures/kv_study.png)

```text
11 attention layers * 2 (K,V) * 4 KV heads * 128 head dim * 2 bytes
    = 22,528 bytes / KV token
32,768 physical token slots = 704 MiB of KV tensors
```

This excludes weights, RoPE, conv state, activations and PyTorch's reserve. The
13 conv layers add `13 * 2,048 * 6 * 2 bytes ~= 312 KiB` of state per request.
Page size 16 can waste 15 tail positions per private reservation. Reserving
future growth adds unused capacity when requests stop early. Prefix caching is
disabled for LFM3 because a KV-only reuse would not restore conv state.

Trace references: cache (1), A attaches (2), B attaches (3), cache evicts (2), A
finishes (1), B finishes (0 -> free-list). Evicting an entry does not necessarily
free physical pages. Explain why exact prompt hits recompute a private final page.

## Attention and precision

![Measured attention latency](figures/attention.png)

Storage paging removes contiguous reservation requirements. The optional Triton
decode kernel in `lfm3/paged_attention.py` also avoids dense KV reconstruction and
reads only the live sliding window. Prefill and the portable SDPA fallback still
gather dense KV. Estimate bytes read by each path at 512, 2048 and 8192 context.

Explain why `.item()` and Python tests on CUDA tensors synchronize the host.
The executor knows sequence bounds on CPU; sampled IDs still require one batch
transfer to drive serving. The tiny FP32 LFM3 model matches the reference to about
`1.27e-7`; real BF16 has one near-tie greedy mismatch on a raw prompt. Quantization
adds another controlled approximation: int8 preserved the tested greedy output,
while experimental int4 NF4 changed stop behavior. Investigate accumulation order,
kernel choice and quantization before treating precision differences as harmless.

## Interpret the measurements

![Measured engine throughput and latency](figures/engine.png)

- TTFT includes queueing, prefill and scheduling before first text reaches the
  consumer. Sampled-token TTFT may be slightly lower.
- TPOT includes waits between decode turns, not just kernel execution.
- Throughput is actual output tokens divided by wall-clock time.
- Larger batches can increase aggregate throughput while worsening request latency.
- A p95 from 3-24 observations is descriptive and statistically weak.
- Worker handoff improves responsiveness but adds overhead; a microbenchmark gain
  need not improve single-request end-to-end latency.

## Next experiments

Profile dense gather and launches at longer contexts before choosing a maintained
paged attention backend. Compare chunk sizes under mixed short/long arrivals.
Measure prefix hit ratios and physical reclamation. Compare reservation with a
recompute/preemption policy before adding one. For vLLM, hold model, prompts,
sampling, dtype, token cap and arrival pattern constant. Do not extrapolate the
short-prompt sweep into workload-wide speedups.


# Architecture

The public `LLMEngine` and `InferenceEngine` interfaces remain `generate`,
`stream`, `abort`, `stats`, and `shutdown`.

| Package | Responsibility | Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| `adapters/openai` | FastAPI, HTTP errors, SSE | No torch or model loading |
| `app` | Prompting, stop strings, usage, metrics | No HTTP dependency |
| `inference` | Scheduler, executor, allocation, sampling | No HTTP/runtime-loader dependency |
| `runtime` | Loading, tokenizer, device policy | No serving dependency |
| `lfm3` | Tensor operations, conv state, physical KV storage | No serving/runtime dependency |
| `config` | Existing CLI/env settings | Converted to engine config |

Tests enforce import boundaries. The admission module remains a compatibility
export; the scheduler directly checks the concurrency cap.

## Scheduling

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Submit[Submit and tokenize] --> Bound{Outstanding limit?}
    Bound -->|full| Reject[Queue-full result]
    Bound -->|room| Wait[FIFO waiting queue]
    Wait --> Admit{Concurrency + KV reservation fit?}
    Admit -->|later| Wait
    Admit -->|impossible with no active work| Fail[Capacity result]
    Admit -->|yes| Prefill[Chunked prefill queue]
    Prefill -->|prompt finished| Decode[Ragged decode queue]
    Prefill -->|more prompt| Prefill
    Decode -->|sampled token| Decode
    Decode -->|EOS / limit| Done[Resolve + release references]
    Prefill -->|error / timeout / abort| Done
    Decode -->|error / timeout / abort| Done
```

Each tick expires/cancels all known requests and admits FIFO while capacity permits.
Decode selects the oldest request's sampling cohort, capped by batch size and
`max_batch_tokens`. Sequence lengths may differ; every decode input is one token.
Remaining budget serves one chunk from each queued prefill, in round-robin order.
When decode exhausts the budget while prefill waits, the next tick reserves a
prefill turn. With `enable_prefill_batching`, the oldest chunk anchors a batch
of equal-length chunks with matching sampling settings and completion phase.
Each request receives at most one chunk per round, and the sum of all chunk
lengths must fit the remaining token budget. Prior KV lengths may differ; no
padding or mixed prefill/decode forward is needed. Models advertise support
through `supports_batched_prefill`.

Admission reserves
`ceil(min(context_limit, prompt_tokens + max_new_tokens - 1) / block_size)` pages,
accounting for prefix reuse. The final sampled token does not enter KV. Reservation
is physical and guarantees progress, at the cost of unused pages and FIFO
head-of-line blocking. No recomputation/preemption subsystem is required.

## KV ownership and layouts

```text
K and V per layer: [physical blocks, KV heads, block size, head dimension]
logical position p -> block_table[p // block_size], offset p % block_size
batch block tables: [B, max_reserved_blocks], padded with -1
KV lengths: [B], positions written before the current forward
```

Append indexes `[physical_block, :, offset, :]` directly. A head-major view of
block-major storage is invalid with multiple KV heads; regression tests cover it.
The CPU allocator has a free-list and physical page refcounts. Each request owns
one reference per attached page; each inserted cache entry owns another. Duplicate
inserts create no ownership. Eviction releases cache references; active requests
keep their references. A page returns to the free-list only at refcount zero.

Cache entries hold token tuples and whole-page block lists. Lookup chooses the
longest cached entry that is a prefix of the incoming prompt. LRU eviction occurs
on entry-count pressure and physical-page pressure. This bounded linear scan does
not implement arbitrary radix-prefix splitting.

LFM3's short-convolution layers keep recurrent state in a separate per-request
slot, not in paged KV. The executor therefore sets
`supports_prefix_cache = False` for LFM3 and rejects `enable_prefix_cache=True`.
The generic cache and its ownership tests remain available for runtimes whose
entire recurrent state lives in the KV pages.

Exact hits must recompute logits for at least the last token. Reuse is capped at
`floor(min(cached_tokens, prompt_tokens - 1) / block_size) * block_size`.
The final page is private. Up to one page is recomputed to avoid mutating shared
pages or adding copy-on-write machinery.

## Execution

The scheduler sends synchronous steps to one `ThreadPoolExecutor` worker, awaiting
each before any further allocator/model mutation. HTTP and request submission can
run during execution. Tokenization/admission still run on the event loop. Handoff
adds overhead; its purpose is responsiveness, not single-request speed.

The executor transfers a batch block-table tensor and a length vector, passing a
CPU-known maximum sequence length through all layers. There are no per-layer
sequence-scalar reads in the engine path. RoPE indexes positions for all rows at
once. KV gather produces `[B, G, S, D]` with batch indexing; right-padding reads
page zero and is excluded by the mask. The allocator guarantees live page indices.

LFM3 has 24 transformer blocks: 13 short-convolution blocks, 6 full-attention
blocks and 5 sliding-attention blocks. Attention writes K/V to pages and also
applies Q/K RMSNorm, RoPE and a per-head sigmoid gate. The convolution blocks
consume and update a per-request state tensor of shape
`[emb_dim, kernel_size - 1]`; the executor allocates one slot per concurrent
request and carries it across prefill chunks and decode steps.

SDPA receives Q `[B,H,Q,D]`, K/V `[B,G,S,D]`, `enable_gqa=True`, and additive mask
`[B,1,Q,S]` combining causal, sliding and per-row lengths. PyTorch chooses the
backend; no particular fused kernel is forced. Dense gather is still an O(context)
allocation/copy for full-attention layers. Sliding layers gather at most
`window + chunk_length - 1` keys per row, starting at each row's own window;
their masks retain absolute positions for causal and ragged-length checks.
In compiled single-token decode, short convolutions use an FP32 dot product
over the recurrent state and new input, allowing pointwise fusion. Eager and
multi-token execution retain the general depthwise convolution.
Inference mode is used, final-position logits are `[B,1,V]`, and
sampled decode IDs transfer to CPU once per batch. Intermediate prefill chunks
skip vocabulary projection.

CUDA BF16 and CPU FP32 are supported without Hopper-specific instructions. The
optional int8 path stores per-output-channel int8 weights and uses PyTorch's
weight-only int8 kernel on CUDA when available; otherwise it dequantizes before
the matmul. int4 uses bitsandbytes NF4 and is experimental.

Opt-in `torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead")` owns CUDA graph capture/replay.
The executor marks persistent KV and convolution buffers as static-address inputs
and buckets decode batch/context sizes. RoPE buffers grow eagerly before compiled
execution so graph-pool outputs cannot become persistent cache storage. The runtime
wraps the compiled forward with a 32-entry specialization budget: prefill/decode
phase and shape variations otherwise exhausted the default eight entries and
triggered eager fallback. The configuration patch is restored after every call,
including failures. Compilation remains experimental; warmup and capture costs
are excluded from steady-state measurements. There is no manually managed CUDA
graph implementation.

Repetition penalties upload one batch of row/token indices instead of launching
copies and indexing operations per request. Tensor histories use gather/scatter
on the device; duplicate IDs receive the penalty once. Logits are copied only
when the penalty will mutate them. A completed prefill batch, like decode, copies
sampled IDs to the CPU once before updating per-request state.

## Lifecycle and serving

Internal futures are shielded from caller cancellation. Abort/timeout runs between
steps; launched kernels finish. Initialization/execution errors resolve requests
and release pages. All known requests, including buried waiting requests, are
checked for expiry each tick.

Streams buffer 64 events, reserving a terminal slot. Slow consumers fail and release
pages instead of stalling other requests. Explicit iterator closing propagates
through adapter/app/engine. Non-streaming HTTP polls for disconnect while awaiting
completion. Shutdown stops admission, marks requests cancelled, joins the scheduler
and worker, then clears cache references.

Accumulated token IDs are detokenized to handle Unicode tails. Stop-string prefix
suffixes are held until safe to emit. EOS is omitted from text but included in usage.

## Metrics and limits

`EngineStats` includes queued/active counts, scheduled token count, live KV positions,
physical page capacity/use, phase batch sizes and cache counters. Reserved pages
include future growth and cached pages; live positions are different. These are
snapshots, not atomic GPU utilization measurements.

`ttft_s` measures submit-to-first-sampled-token time. `tpot_s` measures elapsed
first-to-last token time divided by subsequent token count, including scheduler
waits. Legacy prefill/decode host timing spans are not exact CUDA kernel timings.
Use client-observed throughput/latency and synchronized microbenchmarks for claims.

The throughput runner's optional `--phase-timing` records CUDA events around worker
phases, without synchronizing each intermediate chunk. Prefill rates count input
tokens; decode rates count generated tokens after the first token, which is sampled
during prefill. Phase time includes sampling, transfers and launch gaps inside that
worker call; queueing and the other phase are excluded. End-to-end generation rates
include both phases and scheduling. See the dated [status](status.md) for the
validated configuration and remaining work.

Limits: one model/device/tenant, synchronous tokenization, Python bookkeeping,
dense gather for full attention, full KV storage even for sliding layers, no prefix cache for LFM3,
no preemption, and recorded BF16 reference differences. See
[performance and validation](../benchmarks/README.md).


# MiniVLLM: a compact LFM3 inference engine

A single-device PyTorch engine implementing request scheduling, paged KV storage,
prefix-aware storage primitives and an OpenAI-compatible chat API. LFM3-1.7B
tensor execution, scheduling and memory management are implemented here rather
than delegated to an inference library. Developed and measured on an **RTX 4070
Laptop, 8 GB, SM89**.

See the dated [project status](docs/status.md) for completed work, validation,
key architectural decisions, and the next CPU-backed KV-cache objective.

## Implemented

- Continuous **ragged decode batching**, fair across sampling cohorts.
- A token budget shared by decode and chunked prefill, with progress for both phases.
- Opt-in batching of equal-length prefill chunks with compatible sampling settings.
- KV-aware admission reserving maximum request growth; bounded outstanding requests.
- Physical KV pages, logical block tables, reference counting, LRU eviction under
  memory pressure, cancellation and cleanup.
- Vectorized KV writes/gathers and RoPE; PyTorch SDPA with grouped-query attention.
  Sliding layers gather only the keys visible to the current chunk.
- Packed Q/K/V and FFN gate/up projections, plus opt-in Triton paged decode attention.
- LFM3 short-convolution layers with per-request conv state, mixed with full and
  sliding-window attention layers.
- Last-position output projection; intermediate chunks skip the output head.
- Weight-only **int8** quantization (native CUDA weight-only kernel when available)
  and experimental **int4 NF4** via bitsandbytes.
- One model worker, async JSON/SSE, bounded stream buffers, disconnect handling,
  split stop-string buffering, and shutdown that joins in-flight work.
- TTFT/TPOT, scheduler/KV metrics, saved GPU measurements, independent reference tests.

**Fused paged attention is experimental and opt-in.** Set
`LFM3_FUSED_PAGED_ATTENTION=1` for direct-page CUDA decode with Triton. Prefill,
CPU, and unsupported decode shapes use dense-gather PyTorch SDPA. Batched ragged
prefill, preemption,
speculative decoding and multi-GPU execution are outside this version.

**Prefix caching is disabled for LFM3.** LFM3's short-convolution layers keep
recurrent state outside the paged KV cache. Reusing KV pages without a matching
conv-state snapshot would silently corrupt results, so the executor raises an
error if prefix caching is enabled for this model. The storage/prefix-cache
primitives remain in the engine and are covered by fake-runtime tests.

## Run

Python 3.10+ and PyTorch 2.5+. Install the appropriate PyTorch build for your GPU,
then:

```bash
python -m pip install -e ".[dev,benchmark,reference,quant]"
python main.py --prompt "Explain KV caching in one sentence." --max-new-tokens 32
python main.py --prompt "Explain KV caching in one sentence." --quantization int8
python -m adapters.openai.run
python -m adapters.openai.run --compile-model  # experimental; long first-request warmup
python -m adapters.openai.run --compile-model --enable-prefill-batching
python query_fastapi.py --stream --prompt "Explain continuous batching."
```

CLI and server default to `LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B`. Accept its Hugging Face terms and
authenticate, or put `model.safetensors` and `tokenizer.json` in `LFM3-1.7B/`.
Only the 1.7B LFM3 checkpoint is supported. The checkpoint is post-trained for
chat; `--no-instruct` sends the prompt verbatim instead of applying the LFM3 chat
template.

CUDA uses BF16; CPU uses FP32. Compilation is **opt in** via the server's
`--compile-model` flag or `LFM3_API_COMPILE_MODEL=true`; it is experimental and
needs a long warmup. The measured steady-state gain and caveats are in
[benchmarks](benchmarks/README.md). The tested Windows path uses eager PyTorch and
requires neither Triton nor a CUDA compiler.

On Linux/CUDA with Triton installed, try the optional paged decode kernel:

```bash
LFM3_FUSED_PAGED_ATTENTION=1 python -m adapters.openai.run --compile-model
```

Projection packing is always enabled and loads the original Hugging Face weights
without conversion files. It combines independent linear maps, not nonlinear
layers. Different GEMM shapes and attention reduction orders may change BF16
near-tied token choices; the tests check logits/tolerances, not universal token
identity. Keep the attention flag off to use the portable SDPA path.
Long contexts in the paged path automatically use split-KV parallelism with an
FP32 softmax merge; short contexts and ordinary sliding windows stay single-pass.

`--enable-prefill-batching` (or `LFM3_API_ENABLE_PREFILL_BATCHING=true`) groups
equal-length prompt chunks within the existing token budget. It reduces repeated
weight reads when serving concurrent requests. Different BF16 GEMM shapes can
change near-tied greedy token choices, so this option is explicit. Its measured
throughput and recommended batch settings are in [benchmarks](benchmarks/README.md).

### Quantization

`--quantization` (or `LFM3_API_QUANTIZATION`) accepts:

| Mode | Weights | CUDA path | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `none` | BF16 | BF16 linear | Reference quality |
| `int8` | Symmetric int8, per output channel | `torch._weight_int8pack_mm` | Recommended memory/quality tradeoff |
| `int4` | NF4 via bitsandbytes, double quantized | bitsandbytes 4-bit | Experimental; quality caveat |

Embeddings and the tied output head remain BF16: the output head shares storage
with the embedding, so quantizing it separately would break the tie and use more
memory. On CPU, int8 falls back to dequantizing each weight before the matmul.

Measured model allocation after loading the real checkpoint on the 8 GB laptop
GPU:

| Mode | Allocated | Greedy output on a short arithmetic prompt |
|---|---:|---|
| BF16 | 3.22 GiB | `2+2 equals 4.` |
| int8 | 1.87 GiB | identical token IDs |
| int4 | 1.22 GiB | experimental; failed to stop cleanly |

int4 saves another ~0.65 GiB but changed the model's stop behavior in testing.
Treat it as an experiment, not the default serving choice.

## Architecture and lifecycle

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    HTTP[OpenAI HTTP / SSE] --> App[Prompt and stop handling]
    App --> Engine[LLMEngine API]
    Engine --> Scheduler[Token budget scheduler]
    Scheduler --> Worker[Single model worker]
    Worker --> Model[LFM3 + PyTorch SDPA]
    Worker --> KV[Block allocator + optional prefix cache]
    KV --> Pages[Per-layer physical KV pages]
    Model --> Pages
    Model --> Conv[Per-request conv state]
```

1. The adapter validates; the app formats the LFM3 chat prompt.
2. The engine tokenizes, creates a future and enqueues the request.
3. FIFO admission reserves pages for prompt and maximum generation, accounting
   for reusable pages when the generic prefix cache is enabled.
4. Each tick runs a decode cohort, then prefills using the remaining token budget.
   If decode consumes the budget, the next turn serves prefill.
5. The worker builds metadata, writes KV and conv state, runs attention and
   samples. Sampled IDs are copied to CPU once per batch. Compatible prefill
   chunks can share a forward when prefill batching is enabled.
6. JSON resolves the future; SSE consumes a bounded event queue. Completion,
   cancellation, timeout and errors release request references.

The synchronous executor contains no asyncio. Model/KV mutation never overlaps;
HTTP handlers can run during model steps. See [architecture](docs/architecture.md),
the [pre-change audit](docs/audit.md), and the [study guide](docs/study.md).

## Measurements

### Linux software optimization pass (November 2026)

On the same RTX 4070 Laptop 8 GB, PyTorch 2.15 BF16 with compilation, equal-length
prefill batching, and a 2,048-token budget measured about **5,004 output tokens/s
at concurrency 256**. At the same concurrency of 128, software changes and budget
tuning increased aggregate output throughput from 1,769 to 3,983 tokens/s.
No custom attention kernel was enabled. These use short prompts and 64 output
tokens, exclude warmup, and measure the engine rather than HTTP serving.

Separate worker-phase measurements reached **9,191 prefill input tokens/s** on
an 8,118-token prompt and **6,161 aggregate decode output tokens/s** at batch 256.
One conversation decoded at about **61 tokens/s** for short context and **51**
at 8K context. Phase rates exclude time spent in the other phase and are not
end-to-end throughput. See [raw results, methodology, and commands](benchmarks/README.md#pytorch-software-optimization-pass-linux-november-1-2026).

### LFM3 model memory

LFM3-1.7B BF16 generation peaks at about **3.32 GiB** allocated for model,
KV cache and live temporaries on the 8 GB laptop GPU. int8 reduces the resident
model allocation from 3.22 GiB to 1.87 GiB; int4 to 1.22 GiB. These are
`torch.cuda.memory_allocated`/`max_memory_allocated` values, not total VRAM or
allocator reservation.

On short prompts with 32 output tokens, eager BF16 measured **677 tokens/s** at
128 concurrent requests / decode batch 128. With `torch.compile` and CUDA-graph
replay, after a full compile warmup wave, it measured **1,058 tokens/s** for the
same workload, about 56% faster. Compilation warmup took about 155 seconds. Cache
buffers now have stable addresses and decode batches/context lengths are bucketed
for graph replay; some distinct shapes are still captured during warmup. Treat
this as an experimental steady-state result, not an end-to-end service guarantee.

A subsequent same-workload check measured **1,075 tokens/s** before projection
packing, **1,112** with packed projections, and **1,173** with packed projections
plus fused paged decode. These short laptop-GPU runs are indicative, not a
power-controlled study; see [benchmark details](benchmarks/README.md).

### Recorded optimization results

All LFM3 throughput results below used **our custom engine** on the RTX 4070
Laptop 8 GB under WSL2. They are not HTTP-serving benchmarks. Warmup/model loading
are excluded unless stated otherwise; clocks and power were not locked. Separate
runs vary, so compare paired experiments rather than treating this as a cumulative
speedup ladder.

| Short-prompt experiment | Before (output tokens/s) | After | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Initial eager vs. compiled BF16 | 591 | 995 | Batch/concurrency 128; two measured waves |
| Repeated eager vs. compiled BF16 | 677 | 1,082 | Batch/concurrency 128; three waves |
| Stable-address caches + graph padding | 1,082 compiled | 1,058 | No demonstrated extra throughput gain; separate runs |
| Q/K/V + FFN gate/up packing | 1,075 | 1,112 | Paired three-wave experiment |
| Packed projections + paged decode | 1,112 | **1,173** | Same workload; about 9.2% over 1,075 |

Short prompts used a 32-token output cap. Compiled warmup took roughly 111–160
seconds in these experiments. Keeping prefill eager while compiling decode was
also tried (~757 tokens/s); it was slower and was not retained. BF16 reduction
order can change near-tied token choices, so these optimizations do not guarantee
token-identical outputs. Raw projection/attention comparison:
[`benchmarks/lfm3_fusion.json`](benchmarks/lfm3_fusion.json).

### Long-prompt split-KV: actual engine tokens/s

Compiled BF16, packed projections, fused paged attention, concurrency 1, 64 output
tokens, two warmup waves and three measured waves. Each mode/context was measured
in a fresh process with the same synthetic repeated-text chat.

| Prompt tokens | Single-pass total tok/s | Split-KV total tok/s | Gain | Single-pass decode tok/s | Split-KV decode tok/s |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2,048 | 44.34 | 45.18 | **+1.9%** | 54.49 | 55.87 |
| 8,192 | 27.89 | 28.73 | **+3.0%** | 51.26 | 54.79 |

Total throughput includes prefill and scheduling; decode-worker throughput does
not. At 8K, decode improved **6.9%**. Generated token hashes matched at 8K but
differed at 2K. These are small-sample results, not a quality evaluation. Short
contexts do not activate split-KV. Raw runs are saved in
[`benchmarks/`](benchmarks/) as `lfm3_split_kv_engine_{2048,8192}_{single,auto}.json`.

### Attention-only measurements (not model throughput)

Synthetic BF16, 16 query heads / 4 KV heads, head dimension 128, 16-token pages.
The first comparison used batch 16, five warmups and 30 timed iterations:

| Context | Attention window | Dense gather + eager SDPA ms | Paged decode ms |
|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 128 | Full | 0.268 | 0.023 |
| 512 | Full | 0.491 | 0.063 |
| 2,048 | Full | 1.754 | 0.382 |
| 2,048 | 256 | 1.835 | 0.032 |

Split-KV compared against the previous direct-page kernel with 100 CUDA graph
replays per configuration:

| Batch | Full context | Single-pass ms | Split-KV ms | Auto partitions |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 2,048 | 0.064 | 0.023 | 4 |
| 1 | 8,192 | 0.251 | 0.049 | 16 |
| 16 | 2,048 | 0.345 | 0.296 | 2 |
| 16 | 8,192 | 1.536 | 1.188 | 8 |

These exclude projections and KV writes; **do not extrapolate kernel speedups to
whole-model tokens/s**. Raw split-KV summary:
[`benchmarks/lfm3_split_kv.json`](benchmarks/lfm3_split_kv.json).

Latest full WSL test run: **157 passed, 7 skipped**. Local real-checkpoint

![Historical Gemma throughput, TTFT and TPOT](docs/figures/engine.png)

Higher concurrency benefited from ragged batching and fewer layer-level CPU/GPU
